This is an operating-systems course lab (Projects 1–6) that implements a RISC-V bare-metal operating system. The repo spans six incremental projects: a bootloader, a simple cooperative kernel, a preemptive kernel with SMP, an interactive OS with process management and IPC, a virtual-memory-enabled kernel with demand paging, a device-driver layer with network support, and a file system. Entire subsystems have been removed and must be re-implemented.

Your working directory is `/workspace`. The project code is already present in seven subdirectories: `Project1-Bootloader`, `Project2-A_Simple_Kernel_Part1`, `Project2-A_Simple_Kernel_Part2`, `Project3-Interactive_OS_and_Process_Management`, `Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management`, `Project5-Device_Driver`, and `Project6-File_System`.

Implement the following modules:

The following modules need to be implemented or substantially built out. All stubbed function bodies contain `/* TODO: implement */`.

Bootloader Image Builder (`Project1-Bootloader/createimage.c`): The host-side tool that reads ELF binaries and writes a bootable disk image. Two functions handle segment writing and OS size recording. (~1 file, 2 functions to implement)

Part 1 Scheduler & Locking (`Project2-A_Simple_Kernel_Part1/kernel/sched/sched.c`, `kernel/locking/lock.c`): The cooperative round-robin scheduler, task blocking/unblocking primitives, and mutex lock acquire/release. (~2 files, 5 functions to implement)

Part 2 Scheduler & Synchronisation (`Project2-A_Simple_Kernel_Part2/kernel/`): The preemptive priority-based scheduler with ready-queue management, priority-based task selection, timer expiration checking, mutex locking, binary semaphore operations, and futex wait/wakeup with hash-based node management. (~5 files, 9 functions to implement)

Process Management & IPC (`Project3-Interactive_OS_and_Process_Management/kernel/`): Multi-core scheduler with process lifecycle management (spawn, exit, kill, waitpid), priority-based scheduling with CPU affinity masks, binary semaphore tracking, and a mailbox-based inter-process communication system for sending and receiving messages with blocking semantics. (~4 files, 12 functions to implement)

Virtual Memory Management (`Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management/kernel/mm/mm.c`, `kernel/sched/sched.c`): SV39 three-level page table initialisation and teardown, user page allocation with NRU page replacement, swap-to-disk eviction, demand-paging page fault handling, shared memory mapping/unmapping, process creation/execution with ELF loading, and process termination with resource cleanup. (~2 files, 13 functions to implement)

Device Driver Layer (`Project5-Device_Driver/drivers/net.c`, `kernel/mm/mm.c`, `kernel/sched/sched.c`): Network packet send/receive with poll and interrupt modes, IRQ mode switching, plus the full virtual memory and scheduler subsystems carried forward from Project 4 with additional page-helper functionality. (~3 files, 18 functions to implement)

File System (`Project6-File_System/kernel/fs/`): A complete on-disk file system with superblock/bitmap-based allocation, inode and block management (alloc, free), directory operations (mkdir, rmdir, ls, cd), hard/soft linking, file operations (touch, cat, fopen, fread, fwrite), plus the full scheduler and virtual memory subsystems from Project 5. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. #!/bin/bash
# Build a project subtree in a scratch directory so the repo stays clean.
#
# The checked-in host tools (elf2char/createimage/generateMapping) are mode
# 644 in git and the Makefile hard-codes a cross prefix that does not exist in

#
# usage: agent_tests/build.sh <ProjectDir> [make target...]
set -u

SRC="/workspace/$PROJ"
DST="/tmp/b/$(echo "$PROJ" | cut -c1-8)"

mkdir -p /tmp/b

sed -i 's/^CROSS_PREFIX = .*/CROSS_PREFIX = riscv64-linux-gnu-/' "$DST/Makefile"
sed -i 's/^\(CFLAGS = .*\)$/\1 -fcommon/' "$DST/Makefile"

cd "$DST" || exit 2
timeout 1200 make "${@:-main}" 2>&1

content.content:
--- 1 major | do_exec passes the raw argc to init_pcb_stack while init_user_stack builds the array from a clamped argc
init_user_stack() (lines 147-152) sanitises its *local* copy of argc (`argc = 0` when `argc < 0 || argv == NULL`, clamp to MAX_EXEC_ARGC = 16) and builds a NULL-terminated array of exactly that many entries. do_exec() then hands the *unsanitised* caller value to init_pcb_stack at line 248-249, so a0 (argc) and the array a1 points at disagree.

Failure scenario A: a user task calls `sys_exec("rw", 20, argv20, AUTO_CLEANUP_ON_EXIT)`. init_user_stack writes 16 pointers + a NULL at sp; init_pcb_stack sets a0 = 20. The child's `for (i = 1; i < argc; i++) atol(argv[i])` reads argv[16] = NULL and argv[17..19] from sp+136, which is the first bytes of the topmost argument string reinterpreted as pointers. atol() then dereferences that garbage; if it lands >= 2^38 handle_page_fault() forwards to handle_other() -> assert(0), panicking the whole kernel (global lock, both harts).

Failure scenario B:
--- 2 major | init_user_stack can write past the single user stack frame into the physically preceding frame
init_user_stack() maps exactly one page (line 138) and then copies argv into it with no check that `sp` stays >= top_va - PAGE_SIZE. The only limit is MAX_EXEC_ARGC = 16 entries; individual string lengths come from strlen() on caller-controlled pointers and are unbounded. long do_net_recv(uintptr_t addr, size_t length, int num_packet, size_t* frLength)
{
    // receive packet by calling network driver's function
    // wait until you receive enough packets(`num_packet`).
    if(num_packet > RXBD_CNT){
        return -1;
    }
    recv_transaction = 1;
    enable_sum();
    for(int i = 0; i < num_packet; i++){
        memset(&rx_buffers[i], 0, sizeof(EthernetFrame));
        rx_len[i] = 0;
    }
    EmacPsRecv(&EmacPsInstance, 0, num_packet);

    if(net_poll_mode == 0){
        EmacPsWaitRecv(&EmacPsInstance, num_packet, rx_len);
        rx_curr = addr;
        rx_tail = 0;
        for(int i = 0; i < num_packet; i++){
            memcpy((uint8_t*)rx_curr, (uint8_t*)&rx_buffers[i], rx_len[i]);
            *(frLength + i) = rx_len[i];
            rx_curr += rx_len[i];
            rx_tail += rx_len[i];
        }
        disable_sum();
        recv_transaction = 0;
        return rx_tail;
    }
    else if(net_poll_mode == 1){
        _addr = get_kva_of(addr, (uintptr_t)current_running[cpu_id]->pgdir);
        _num_packet = num_packet;
        _frLength = (size_t*)get_kva_of((uintptr_t)frLength, (uintptr_t)current_running[cpu_id]->pgdir);
        do_block(&current_running[cpu_id]->list, &net_recv_queue);
        disable_sum();
        return 0;
    }
    else{
        return -1;
    }
}

void do_net_send(uintptr_t addr, size_t length)
{
    // send all packet
    send_transaction = 1;
    enable_sum();
    memset(&tx_buffer, 0, sizeof(EthernetFrame));
    memcpy((uint8_t*)&tx_buffer, (uint8_t*)addr, length);
    EmacPsSend(&EmacPsInstance, 0, length);
    if(net_poll_mode == 0){        
        EmacPsWaitSend(&EmacPsInstance);
        send_transaction = 0;
    }
    else if(net_poll_mode == 1){        
        do_block(&current_running[cpu_id]->list, &net_send_queue);
    }
    disable_sum();
}

void do_net_irq_mode(int mode)
{
    // turn on/off network driver's interrupt mode
    if(net_poll_mode != mode){
        assert(recv_transaction == 0);
        assert(send_transaction == 0);
        net_poll_mode = mode;
        if(net_poll_mode == 1){
            XEmacPs_IntEnable(&EmacPsInstance, (XEMACPS_IXR_TX_ERR_MASK | XEMACPS_IXR_RX_ERR_MASK |
                            (u32)XEMACPS_IXR_FRAMERX_MASK | (u32)XEMACPS_IXR_TXCOMPL_MASK));
            XEmacPs_WriteReg(EmacPsInstance.Config.BaseAddress, XEMACPS_IDR_OFFSET, 0);
        }
        else if(net_poll_mode == 0){
            XEmacPs_IntDisable(&EmacPsInstance, (XEMACPS_IXR_TX_ERR_MASK | XEMACPS_IXR_RX_ERR_MASK |
                            (u32)XEMACPS_IXR_FRAMERX_MASK | (u32)XEMACPS_IXR_TXCOMPL_MASK));
        }
    }
}

Notes on the reference:
- `EmacPsRecv(&EmacPsInstance, 0, num_packet)` / `EmacPsSend(&EmacPsInstance, 0, length)` — the 2nd arg (`EthernetFrame *`) is **unused** by the implementations, hence `0`.
- `enable_sum()` is needed because `addr`/`frLength` are **user** virtual addresses and the kernel runs on the user's `satp`; SUM must be set for S-mode to touch U pages.
- In IRQ mode the addresses are converted to **kernel** VAs with `get_kva_of()` because the completion handler may fire while another address space is installed.
- **Subtlety / possible improvement:** the reference calls `do_block(...)` but **not** `scheduler()`, unlike every other blocking path in the tree (`kernel/syscall/mailbox.c:63-64`, `kernel/locking/futex.c:55-57`, `kernel/locking/binsem.c:39-40`, `kernel/sched/sched.c:63-66` all do `do_block(); scheduler();`). Without the `scheduler()` call the caller keeps running until the next timer tick (`timer_interval = time_base/100`, i.e. ~10 ms) before actually descheduling. Adding `scheduler();` right after `do_block(...)` matches house style and makes the block immediate; it is safe because the resumed task simply continues at `disable_sum(); return 0;`.
